title: The Post-it accident
hook: A glue that failed at sticking became one of the best-known office supplies.
peek: In 1968 a 3M chemist made an adhesive so weak it barely held. It sat unused for years, until a colleague needed a bookmark that would stay put in his hymnal without tearing the page.
lede: In 1968, Spencer Silver, a chemist at 3M, was trying to make a very strong adhesive. He got the opposite: a glue that stuck lightly, peeled off cleanly and could be stuck down again. It was a solution with no problem attached, and for years Silver showed it around the company without finding anyone who needed it.

bullets.text: Art Fry, a 3M product engineer who sang in his church choir, was tired of paper bookmarks falling out of his hymnbook. In the mid-1970s he realised Silver's glue could hold a marker in place and lift off without damage.
3M has long let staff spend part of their working time on projects of their own choosing, and the company often points to Fry's sticky bookmarks as the example of what that freedom can produce.

A 1977 test launch under the name Press 'n Peel sold poorly. In 1978 3M flooded offices in Boise, Idaho, with free samples, and once people had used the notes, most wanted more. They went on sale across the US in 1980.
The story goes that the famous yellow was an accident too: the lab next door happened to have scrap yellow paper on hand. 3M tells it this way, though it is hard to check.
